doc.title: Nancy Wilson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Hearing Basie, Ink Spots and r-and-b on records and radio
summary: No one in her family was in show business; she learned from her father's records and the Columbus r-and-b radio station.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Where did you hear music that you learned to sing these songs?

On the radio. There was no-one in my family who was in show business or knew anything about it. It was a gift. It wasn’t anything that I saw or witnessed or copied or anything like that. It was just there.
Your dad had a Victrola, right?

Oh yeah. We played – he listened to Count Basie. In fact I heard Little Jimmy Scott with – Lionel Hampton, wasn’t it? So I had to be maybe 10, then. But he would listen. And the Ink Spots. I remember he loved the Ink Spots. So basically Daddy was the one who listened to music.

Oh yeah. Billy Eckstine, Little Jimmy Scott. I heard r-and-b at the little – I don’t know what you would call it. It was like a – what was it like? It was a little restaurant, little hangout place where teenagers went. I heard Little Esther and Dinah Washington, Laverne Baker, Ruth Brown. So that’s when I – I had to be maybe 12 or so when I started – when I really recall hearing r-and-b.
Radio was WDKL? Is that the . . . ?
I have no idea. I remember one station in Columbus. It was WVKO.
